settings.eyebrow: Where it fits, and where it doesn't
settings.headline: Where preparation earns its place
settings.body:
Cartilage — helix, conch, daith, industrial — is a different proposition from a lobe, and people who have had both usually say so. Several piercings in one appointment stretch a brief moment into a longer one. And if the last appointment left you dreading the next, arriving prepared is a reasonable thing to want.

A standard lobe is a single, brief moment — the honest answer for that one is in the FAQ below.

settings.matched: Shorter, routine appointments, smaller areas, and anyone starting out who wants to begin considered.
Longer or more sensitive sessions and larger areas — the one most people settle on for regular work.

settings.headline: Most piercing appointments sit at the entry strength
settings.body: None of the three is "better" than another — each is formulated for a different kind of session. A piercing appointment is one of the shortest things in the range, so Clinical is the sensible default and the upper strengths are there for cartilage or a multi-piercing sitting.
settings.note: If you're between two, the lower one is usually the sensible start, and you can move up next time.

settings.heading: Before you buy: ask your piercer first
settings.body: Studios have protocols, and yours may have a view on arriving with anything applied — particularly around a site that has to be marked accurately and cleaned before it is pierced. Ask when you book rather than on the day. If your piercer says no, that settles it. And if you are being pierced by a reputable studio, they will talk you through what to expect anyway, which is worth more than anything we can put on a page.

settings.question: Do I need numbing cream for an ear piercing?
settings.answer: For a standard lobe, most people don't — it is a single brief moment and plenty of people book one without a second thought. The cases where preparation earns its place are cartilage, several piercings in one appointment, or simply wanting to arrive less anxious than last time.

settings.question: Which strength for a piercing?
settings.answer: Clinical is the sensible default — a piercing appointment is one of the shortest sessions in the range. Cartilage or a multi-piercing sitting is where Advanced makes sense. If you're between two, start with the lower one.

settings.question: Is cartilage different from a lobe?
settings.answer: People who have had both generally say so, and cartilage sites — helix, conch, daith, industrial — also take considerably longer to settle afterwards. Your piercer is the right person to talk you through what your specific placement involves.

settings.question: Will my piercer mind?
settings.answer: Ask when you book. Studios have their own protocols, particularly around a site that has to be marked accurately and cleaned before it is pierced. If your piercer asks you not to use anything, follow that.

settings.question: Can I use it on a nose, navel or nipple piercing?
settings.answer: Senseless is applied to clean, unbroken skin, and it is not for use in or near the eyes or on mucous membranes. Beyond that, your piercer knows the placement and their own protocol — ask them before you book.

settings.question: What about afterwards?
settings.answer: Aftercare is your studio's instruction to give, and a fresh piercing is broken skin — Senseless is not applied to it. Follow the aftercare routine your piercer sets.

settings.headline: Gels
settings.body:
A piercing site is small and exact, which is what gel is for. Three strengths, ordered from the entry tier up.

Gel is usually the format here A piercing site is small and precise, which is what gel is for — it goes exactly where you put it and stays there. Cream is the equal alternative if you prefer its feel. Spray is built for broad areas and is the wrong tool for an earlobe. The same three strengths run across all three formats.
